about.text: I'm Shagar Chandro, a frontend developer based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. I love turning complex problems into simple, beautiful and intuitive interfaces. My focus is on writing clean, maintainable code and building products that feel effortless to use.

projects.title: Aam Bazar
projects.description: A fruit e-commerce concept site with product listing, cart UI and a clean checkout flow.
projects.challenge: Local fruit sellers had no simple way to showcase products online or take orders without relying on third-party marketplace apps.
projects.solution: Built a lightweight storefront with category browsing, a persistent cart and a streamlined checkout — all running on the client with no backend dependency.

projects.title: Amer Hat Bazar
projects.description: A responsive local marketplace landing experience built with vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
projects.challenge: Needed a marketplace-style landing page that felt trustworthy and fast on low-end mobile devices common in the target market.
projects.solution: Focused on a lean CSS footprint, compressed imagery and a mobile-first layout to keep load times low on 3G connections.

projects.title: Personal Home Page
projects.description: An animated personal landing page exploring layout, motion and typography experiments.
projects.challenge: Wanted a sandbox to practice advanced CSS animation and typography without the constraints of a client brief.
projects.solution: Used the page as a personal design lab — scroll-linked motion, variable fonts and layered typography experiments.

projects.title: TextUtils (React)
projects.description: A text-utility React app that trims, converts case and analyzes word/character counts in real time.
projects.challenge: Needed a first real React project to learn component state, props and controlled inputs beyond tutorials.
projects.solution: Built a small but complete utility app — case conversion, whitespace trimming, live word/character counts — all driven by React state.

projects.title: School ERP UI
projects.description: An admin-style dashboard interface concept for managing students, classes and results.
projects.challenge: Small schools often manage records with paper or spreadsheets — a big usability gap for non-technical staff.
projects.solution: Designed a clean, form-heavy admin UI concept covering student records, class assignment and result entry.

projects.title: Portfolio Website
projects.description: This very portfolio — fully responsive, dark/light aware, and backed by a custom admin panel.
projects.challenge: Needed a portfolio that could be updated without touching code, and that felt distinctive rather than templated.
projects.solution: Built a shared localStorage data layer powering both the public site and a full custom admin panel, styled around a code-editor visual identity.

blog.title: How I Built This Portfolio (and Its Admin Panel)
blog.excerpt: A behind-the-scenes look at building a fully static, backend-free portfolio with its own custom CMS.
blog.content:
Most portfolio sites hardcode their content directly into the HTML, which means every small update means editing code. I wanted something different: a single site where all the content — projects, skills, testimonials, everything — lives in one data layer that both the public page and a private admin panel read from.

The result is a shared `DataStore` module backed by `localStorage`. The public site renders every section from it on load; the admin panel reads and writes the exact same structure. No backend, no database, no build step — just HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

The trade-off is that data lives per-browser rather than syncing across devices, so the admin panel includes a JSON export/import tool to back up and restore content reliably.

blog.title: Why I Still Reach for Vanilla JavaScript
blog.excerpt: Frameworks are great, but plain JavaScript still wins for small, fast, dependency-free sites.
blog.content:
It's easy to reach for a framework by default, but for a lot of small projects — landing pages, portfolios, tools — plain JavaScript is genuinely the better choice. No build step, no dependency updates, no bundle size to worry about.

The key is discipline: keep render functions small and predictable, use a single source of truth for state, and lean on the platform (IntersectionObserver, the Fetch API, native form validation) instead of reinventing it.

Frameworks earn their keep on large, stateful applications. For a fast, focused site, vanilla JS keeps things simple and easy to reason about.

blog.title: My Responsive Design Checklist
blog.excerpt: A quick checklist I run through on every project before calling it "done".
blog.content:
Before I consider any layout finished, I run through the same short checklist: test at 375px, 768px, 1024px and 1440px; check that tap targets are at least 44px; make sure text never overflows its container; verify images have explicit dimensions to avoid layout shift; and confirm keyboard focus order makes sense.

It sounds basic, but consistently doing it catches the majority of responsive bugs before a client ever sees them.
